title_en: A Promise Is Not a Padlock
deck_zh: 答应时，对方还没来得及安排什么，那句话已经有分量。后来真的走了，留下的影响也不会跟着消失。承诺的难处，在这两头。
deck_en: A promise matters before anyone has relied on it. Its effects can also outlast the person who made it. Neither truth turns another person’s future into something we own.
body_zh: 老林和老许年轻时合租过一间屋子。后来各自成家，仍在每个月第一个周六吃一顿饭。二十年里，谁也没郑重说过：这是我们的约定。到了那一天，一个往店里走，一个推门进来，饭就吃上了。
有一年，老许的父亲住院。老林说，这一个月，我每天替你去送饭。老许听了，才把那个月的班排满。事情从一句话长成了一张排班表，也长成了病房里每天有人送来的热饭。
先把时间停在排班之前。老林刚说完，老许还没有据此调整任何事，那句话有没有分量？当然有。不然，承诺就只能等别人用了以后才算数，答应的那一刻反而是空的。可答应过的人知道：有些事已经不一样了。
这种分量，不必解释成对方从此拥有了我的明天。它首先在我这里。我还认这句答应，还把自己放在答应过的位置上，就不能一边说它仍然算数，一边把它当作从未发生。后来碰上更急的事，可能只能先做另一件，但没有做的这一件，不会因此变成没答应过。
这也不是说，人要时时刻刻想着那句话，它才有效。睡着了，暂时忘了，忙得没有重新表态，都不自动取消先前的承担。承诺不是每天清零、每天续费的东西；只是到了该做的时候，终究要由今天这个人去做。
## 三件事，别揉成一件
可以先分开看：当时到底说了什么；我现在还认不认、有没有改；那句话已经在别人生活里留下了什么。这三件事相连，却不能互相代替。
说过的话，不是我后来否认就没有了。老许可以记得那句话，也可以拿出聊天记录。但记录能说明老林答应过，不能独自证明他当时心里是否认真，更不能证明他今天究竟怎样理解自己的改变。旁人看得到言行，不因此就看穿了一个人。
现在还认不认，也和这一次做没做到不同。老林某天没去，是自己病倒了，还是两个人商量好了换别人去，还是没有说明就没去？这些要查。不能看见一次没来，就断言从头到尾都是假的；也不能只说一句“我仍然认”，便把当天没送到的饭说没了。
更不能漏掉第三件。老许照着那句答应排了班。老林后来改变主意，这张排班表不会自动恢复原样。谁接手、怎样另作安排、已经发生的耽搁怎么面对，仍是留下来的事情。这不是一笔保证可以算清的债，也不自动变成老林必须无限留下的理由；但一句“我现在不这么想了”，确实没有替老许处理这些事。
所以，改变和悄悄撂下并不一样。改变可以说清：我曾经答应，后来什么变了，我现在不能或不愿继续，已经留下什么。撂下则是在方便的时候，把旧话悄悄放到一边，仿佛它不再值得提。这一层有些只有本人知道。我们可以指出没有做到，可以追问，可以根据痕迹怀疑，却不宜把怀疑写成一个人的终身判词。
这套解释不把承诺写成一笔欠对方的履行义务，而把约束放在自己仍认可的承担和已经留下的现实影响上。这是在回答约束从哪里来，并不是说所有主张对他人负有义务的承诺理论，都已被驳倒。这里谈的是人与人之间的答应，不是替合同、法律或职务责任作解释。它也不是给失信找轻巧的出口：恰恰因为没有一句“都结清了”可说，离开才仍然要面对自己做过的事。
## 二十年，也不能替人签字
再回到每月那顿饭。有一年，老许搬去另一个城市，打电话说，以后可能来不了了。老林心里空了一块。二十年，不是改一下日历就过去的。那家店、那张桌子、每到周六腾出来的半天，都已经嵌进了他的生活。
这能不能证明，老许二十年前就答应过永远来？不能。没有说出口的承诺当然可能存在，也可能在来往中慢慢长成。可是，二十年这一长度，不能单独把习惯变成承诺。老许也可能是每一次都愿意来，并没有把以后都答应下来。
所谓默契，不必因此从语言里删除。临时出差时怎样通知，没赶来时怎样接住，下一次怎样重新安排，都是可以看的材料。我们可以说，两个人似乎早已把那顿饭放进了彼此的日子；不能只凭“你一直这样”，替其中一人宣布“所以你早已答应了”。这两句话，只差一点，越过去的却是别人的那一边。
没有证明他承诺过，也不等于老林的失落是假的。二十年留下的依靠是真的。这份依靠需要慢慢改写，却不因此赋予老林一个把老许叫回来的永久理由。承认影响，和要求对方继续，是两回事。
老林也曾对自己发誓戒烟，并告诉过老许。老许于是知道了，后来不再给他递烟。这里又有一处分界：把打算告诉朋友，不一定是在向朋友作承诺。老林后来改了，不能假装自己没说过，也得承认朋友据此作过安排；但不能仅凭“我听你说过”，便把那项对自己的决定变成对老许的答应。
一个只涉及自己的承诺，后来的人认真面对旧决定，再决定修改，可以完成这次修订。已经向另一个人作出的承诺，自己的改变却不能替别人那一侧结账。两者都不是随口作废，只是留下来的东西不同。
## 留下，和留得住
我们常拿“稳定”夸一段关系。但稳定至少还需要问一句：每个人是为什么留下？有人仍愿意守着答应过的事；有人没有承诺什么，却一回回选择继续。也有人只是走不开，或者一直拖着，或者某个原本有意思的习惯已经空了，身体还沿着旧路走。外表都可以是多年未变。
不能因为关系维持了很久，就证明两边都还有自己的根据；也不能因为我们看不清，就断言双方都没有。原来只有代价和拖延的一端，后来可能重新找到愿意留下的理由；原来真心愿意的一端，也可能慢慢只剩惯性。这不是预言哪一段迟早会散，更不是给所有长久关系排座次。
承诺不能替明天签字，但现实里，人确实可能把别人的路封住。拿“走了就是背叛”给一次离开预先定性，和宣布“你走，我就让你在这一行做不下去”，已经不是同一种动作。后者开始向外加上惩罚和压力。再往前，扣证件、隔绝求助，或把后果抬到让人实际无法脱身，便不是承诺有多重的问题，而是人的基本退出空间被封死了。
也要分清，别人收回自己的参与，使我更难安排生活，并不因此等于他在封我的路；退出本来就可能带来损失。要看他是否另外向外施加惩罚、孤立，把我的拒绝、求助和离开变得更难，甚至不可达。害怕、难过、损失本身，都不能代替对这些具体事情的核对。
自己对自己也有类似的危险。戒烟的决定可以很坚定，同时允许以后认真重问；也可以变成一句不准再碰的终审：“我发过誓，所以任何想改的念头都不用听。”只是先责备自己软弱，和修改的那一步根本到不了，仍要分开。嘴上说“可以改”，实际却从没有一条能改的路，也不算真的留下了空间。
那“我永远不会离开你”还能不能说？可以认真地说，它表达的是此刻愿意站在哪里，不是一份替未来所有时刻代签的文件。后来改变，也不倒过来证明那时的认真必定虚假。只是，越重的话越不能在用完之后假装没有说过；而听到的人，也不能拿那句话把对方重新关回去。承诺不是因为不能担保永远就没有分量，也不是因为有分量，就能把一个人的后来全部收走。
老许搬家以后，也许还会回来吃饭，也许不会。老林替他送过的饭，没有因此白送；老许说过的答应，也没有因为后来改变就变成从来不存在。承诺的重量不在于把一个人永远钉在原地，而在于他今天仍认它时，认真做；真的改了或走了，也不假装自己的脚步从未经过别人的生活。
body_en: Lin and Xu shared a flat when they were young. They eventually married and moved into separate homes, but kept meeting for lunch on the first Saturday of each month. For twenty years nobody formally proposed this arrangement. The date came around; one of them walked into the restaurant; the other was already there.

When Xu’s father went into hospital, Lin offered to deliver his meals every day for a month. Xu then accepted a full schedule of shifts at work. A sentence had become part of a rota, and part of the hospital’s daily life.

But pause the story before Xu changes his schedule. Lin has just spoken. Nobody has relied on him yet. Does his promise already matter? If its force came entirely from reliance, it would have no weight at this moment. Yet making a promise is not usually like mentioning tomorrow’s weather. Something has happened on the speaker’s side too.

Lin has taken a stand: this is something he undertakes to do. While he continues to stand there, he cannot both maintain that undertaking and treat it as if it never existed. An emergency may prevent him from delivering a meal. It does not retroactively remove the promise from the situation he must face.

This need not require constant attention. A promise does not expire whenever its maker sleeps, forgets it for an afternoon, or fails to issue a fresh declaration. What persists is the undertaking, unless it is changed or left. What cannot be supplied in advance is tomorrow’s act: the person who wakes up tomorrow still has to perform it.
## What was said, what still stands, what remains

Three questions help here. What did someone actually say or do? Do they still stand behind it, and what have they revised? What effects has it already had in another person’s life? These questions belong together, but no one of them answers the other two.

Xu can remember the offer or produce the message in which it was made. Lin’s later denial cannot make that evidence disappear. Evidence of the words, however, does not give an observer direct access to Lin’s sincerity at the time, or to the way he understands his change of mind now.

Suppose a meal fails to arrive. Was Lin ill? Had the two friends agreed that somebody else would go? Did he simply not turn up? Those are different accounts of what happened. One missed visit cannot by itself establish that the original offer was a lie. Equally, Lin’s assurance that he remains committed cannot turn an undelivered meal into a delivered one.

The third question is where Xu’s rota comes back in. If Lin changes his mind, Xu’s shifts do not rearrange themselves. Somebody must face the missing meals, the alternative arrangements, any delay already caused. Lin cannot do this merely by announcing that he no longer wishes to continue.

These effects are not a neatly calculable debt, nor do they automatically require him to remain indefinitely, restore every channel of contact, or keep answering without limit. They are real effects that his departure does not settle. Saying that he can leave and saying that nothing remains are quite different claims.

Revision also differs from quietly dropping something when it becomes inconvenient. A revision can acknowledge the former undertaking, what changed, and what has been left behind. Dropping it tries to make the earlier stand disappear from the account. Much of that difference is known from within. From outside, we can report failures, obstacles and agreed changes, ask questions, and make fallible inferences. We should hesitate before turning one failure into a final description of a person.

In this account, a personal promise is not an obligation owed to its recipient. Its force lies in what the speaker genuinely continues to undertake and in effects already left in another person’s life. That is a choice about where binding force comes from, not a demonstration that every theory of directed obligation is false. Nor is it an interpretation of contracts, legal duties or the responsibilities of an office. It offers no convenient excuse for unreliability: the maker cannot escape the past by merely declaring the future different.
## Twenty years cannot sign for someone

Eventually Xu moves to another city. He phones Lin: the monthly lunches may no longer be possible. Lin feels an absence opening in his calendar. Twenty years do not vanish because someone crosses out a recurring appointment. The table, the restaurant and the spare Saturday have become part of his life.

Does this prove that Xu promised, twenty years earlier, to attend forever? No. An unspoken commitment can certainly exist, and can grow gradually. But repetition alone cannot establish it. Xu may have freely chosen each lunch without having undertaken all the lunches still to come.

We need not banish the word understanding from friendship. How the friends handle a missed date, give notice, make room for a work trip, or arrange the next meeting all provide material for describing an implicit commitment. The description remains answerable to what each person actually undertakes. ‘We seem to have made this part of our lives’ is not the same as ‘You have always done it, so I can declare that you promised.’

Nor does uncertainty about a promise make Lin’s loss imaginary. The reliance built over twenty years is real. Xu’s departure does not erase it. But acknowledging that history is different from granting Lin permanent authority to summon him back. A relationship can have consequences without those consequences becoming ownership.

Consider a smaller variation. Lin decides to stop smoking and tells Xu. Xu stops offering him cigarettes. Has a promise to himself now become a promise to his friend? Not necessarily. Reporting an intention is not always undertaking something for the listener. If Lin later revises his decision, he should not pretend Xu never heard about it or made any arrangements. Those are effects of telling him. They do not, by themselves, establish a promise made to Xu.

For an undertaking that concerns only oneself, a later revision which honestly acknowledges the earlier decision can complete the revision. Where a promise has been made to another person, changing one’s own position cannot also settle that other person’s side. The difference is not between serious and disposable promises. It is between what remains in the two situations.
## Staying is not the same as being kept

We often praise a relationship for lasting. Duration deserves another question: what is keeping each person there? One may still stand behind a promise. Another may make no general promise but freely choose to continue. Someone else may be unable to leave, keep postponing a decision, or follow a habit whose original meaning has gone. From a distance, all these arrangements can look equally stable.

Time alone proves none of them. Nor does an observer’s uncertainty prove that neither person has a reason of their own. What began as delay can acquire a freely accepted basis; a freely accepted practice can gradually hollow into inertia. This is not a prediction that certain relationships must collapse. It is a reason to look separately at each end instead of treating ‘the relationship’ as one satisfied person.

A promise cannot own tomorrow. In practice, however, people can make tomorrow’s alternatives unreachable. Calling departure betrayal tries to settle what another person’s departure must mean. Threatening to ruin their livelihood adds pressure directed outward. Withholding identity papers, cutting off help, or imposing consequences that actually prevent escape goes further: it closes a basic way out. These acts cannot be justified simply by pointing to an old promise.

Not every increased difficulty is such an act. Someone withdrawing their own participation may leave me worse off without thereby blocking my departure. We must distinguish that loss from additional punishment or isolation that raises the cost of refusal, seeking help or leaving, perhaps to the point of making a way out inaccessible. Fear alone does not settle which structure is present; concrete circumstances matter.

Something comparable can happen in a promise to oneself. A firm decision to stop smoking may remain open to serious reconsideration. Or ‘I swore I would’ may become an answer that disqualifies every attempt even to ask. Feeling pressure is not yet being unable to revise. Conversely, a declaration that revision is permitted means little when there is no actual route to it.

Can someone still sincerely say, ‘I will never leave you’? Yes, as an expression of where they stand, not as a document signed on behalf of every future moment. A later change does not prove that earlier sincerity was fraudulent. But solemn words cannot simply be discarded after use; nor can their listener use them to shut the speaker back inside. The inability to guarantee forever does not empty a promise of weight. Its weight does not entitle it to possess every later part of a life.

Perhaps Xu will return for occasional lunches. Perhaps he will not. The meals Lin delivered were not made worthless by later change. What Xu once undertook was not made never to have happened. A promise has weight without being a padlock: while I stand behind it, I take it seriously; when I change or leave, I do not pretend that my steps have never passed through somebody else’s life.
